arXiv:2410.04532v1 [math.AP] 06 Oct 2024

Non-radial implosion for the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} and ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}

G. Cao-Labora    J. Gómez-Serrano    J. Shi    G. Staffilani
Abstract

In this paper we construct smooth, non-radial solutions of the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation that develop an imploding finite time singularity, both in the periodic setting and the full space.

1 Introduction

1.1 Historical Background

We consider the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation given by

i​∂tv+Δ​v−v​|v|p−1=0i\partial_{t}v+\Delta v-v|v|^{p-1}=0 (1.1)

for some odd integer pp. Here vv is a complex valued function. Other than the mass, which is the L2L^{2} norm square of vv, the Hamiltonian given by

E⁡(v)=12​∫ℝd|∇v|2+1p+1​∫ℝd|v|p+1E(v)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\nabla v|^{2}+\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|v|^{p+1}

is also conserved. The natural scaling of this equation is given by vλ​(x,t)=λ2/(p+1)​v​(λ​x,λ2​t)v_{\lambda}(x,t)=\lambda^{2/(p+1)}v(\lambda x,\lambda^{2}t), and if vv is a solution, then vλv_{\lambda} is also a solution for any λ>0\lambda>0. Note that if we consider the periodic setting, i.e. the space variable xx belongs to a certain torus 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, then the torus needs to be rescaled appropriately. The critical exponent scs_{c} for which the homogeneous Sobolev norm H˙sc​(ℝd)\dot{H}^{s_{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) remains invariant under scaling is given by sc=d2−2p−1s_{c}=\frac{d}{2}-\frac{2}{p-1}. The goal of this paper is to show that even in the defocusing case, we can exhibit non-radial or periodic blowup for the initial value problem associated to equation (1.1) in the energy supercritical regime, namely when the initial data is in HsH^{s} and s>sc>1s>s_{c}>1.

Before stating precisely the main results, we will touch upon the history of well-posedness and blow up for the initial value problem (1.1) both in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}. At this point the literature is vast hence here we will recall only the few works that are more strictly related to the main results we present below. Let us first review the results in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. In the subcritical case s>scs>s_{c}, local well-posedness was originally proved by Ginibre and Velo [29] using Strichartz estimates, see also [11, 10]. Since in this case the proof shows that the time of existence depends on the HsH^{s} norm of the initial data, for s≤0s\leq 0, using the mass conservation, or for s≤1s\leq 1, using conservation of the Hamiltonian, by iteration global well-posedness in L2L^{2} or H1H^{1} follows easily if the data are respectively in those spaces. On the other hand using the I−I-method, which is based on the concept of almost conserved energies, in certain cases it is possible to extend the local well-posedness to global also below the conserved integrals, see for example [15]. If s=scs=s_{c} local well-posedness is still available via Strichartz estimates using the same techniques in the works mentioned above, but in this case the local time of existence depends also on the profile of the initial data and in order to obtain global well-posedness one needs to treat the problem not as a perturbation of the linear one, but as a truly nonlinear system. The first results in this direction were obtained for the energy critical case (sc=1s_{c}=1), in the 3D radial case [3, 31]. The radial assumption was removed in [16] and in higher dimensions the problem was solved in [53, 65]. For the mass critical problem (sc=0s_{c}=0), global well-posedness in the radial case was proved in [42, 62] , and the radial assumption was removed in [23, 24, 25]. When sc∉{0,1}s_{c}\not\in\{0,1\} the problem is more challenging since a priori the HscH^{s_{c}} norm of the solution is no longer bounded. First in [40] in 3D and later in [49, 67] in all dimensions, the authors proved that if one assumes the uniform boundedness of the HscH^{s_{c}} norm of the solutions then global well-posedness follows. Recently in [26] it was shown that global well-posedness and scattering is available without the a-priori bound in HscH^{s_{c}}. However the data belongs not to HscH^{s_{c}} but to a certain Besov space that scales like HscH^{s_{c}}.

We now address the global well-posedness in supercritical spaces, namely when s<scs<s_{c}. Before the work of [46] there was strong belief that also in the energy supercritical regime, sc>1s_{c}>1, the a priori boundedness of the HscH^{s_{c}} norm should result in global well-posedness. This in fact was conjectured in [4], see also [41, 43]. Numerically such a conjecture was also supported in [17]. In contrast, in [60, 61] models of equation very close to NLS or wave equations at supercritical regimes were proved to exhibit blow-up, while other initial value problem of NLS or wave type with only a logarithmic supercriticality were proved to have global large solutions [58, 44, 18]. Finally, results of norm inflation were obtained for very low supercritical regularity such as in [14, 63].

We now consider well-posedness in the periodic setting. Before the proof of Strichartz estimates by Bourgain in [2] local well-posedness was only known for smooth data, i.e. s>d/2s>d/2, [39, 64]. Strichartz estimates, first partially proved for rational tori [2] and later for all tori [5], allowed for local well-posedness to be proved for subcritical cases s>scs>s_{c}. Also in this case global well-posedness follows if ss is below the mass or energy regularity by iteration as in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. In some cases the I−I-method is still applicable [19, 54] and if the torus is irrational some number theoretical observation can be used to attain global well-posedness for the same range of exponents that gives local well-posedness [33]. Unfortunately at the critical level s=scs=s_{c} the Strichartz estimates have a derivative log\log loss and even local well-posedness is distinctly harder to obtain. One such example is the energy critical problem in 3D (hence quintic nonlinearity) proved to be first locally well-posed in [34] and then globally well-posed in [36]. When the critical exponent sc∉{0,1}s_{c}\not\in\{0,1\} a conditional result similar to that of [41, 43] has been proved in 2D for sc=1/2s_{c}=1/2 in [66].

To the best of our knowledge, before our work there were no results or conjecture concerning blow up for periodic supercritical defocusing initial value problems like (1.1). In fact even in the focusing case the results are very few. We recall [50] in 1D, see also [51], the numerical study in [59], and [52] where the authors extend the log⁡–​log\log–\log blow-up dynamics in [45] to the L2L^{2}-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a domain.

In this paper we are interested in imploding solutions. These are solutions for which the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the function blows up as tt approaches the singularity time. This is in contrast with shock solutions, where the L∞L^{\infty} norm stays bounded and the gradient blows up, which are more ubiquitous in PDE with conservation laws such as compressible Euler or NLS. Specifically, Guderley [32] was the first to construct radial, self-similar imploding singularities for compressible Euler, though non-smooth. See also further work by Jenssen–Tsikkou [37, 38].

Merle–Raphaël–Rodnianski–Szeftel [47] made a breakthrough by constructing the first smooth, radially imploding solutions to the compressible Euler equations. They also extended this work to create imploding singularities for both the compressible Navier-Stokes equations (with decaying density at infinity) [48], and the energy-supercritical defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation [46]. More specifically, they proved that there exists a sequence of scalings rkr_{k} and a sequence of smooth self-similar imploding profiles with such scalings. This was done for almost every value of γ\gamma (the adiabatic exponent relating the pressure to the density). In [7] (see also the review paper [6]), the first two authors together with Buckmaster improved the result to cover all cases of γ\gamma. Moreover, they showed the existence of non-decaying imploding singularities for Navier-Stokes. One of the open questions that Merle–Raphaël–Rodnianski–Szeftel highlight is the construction of nonradial blow-up since their setting only allows for radial perturbations. In [9], we solved this problem. The difficulty introduced by the nonradiality is deep since it essentially turns every ODE analysis into PDE analysis, which is a lot harder. After our work, Chen–Cialdea–Shkoller–Vicol [13] constructed solutions to the 2D compressible Euler equation for which vorticity exhibits finite time blow-up. Chen [12] extended this analysis to any d≥2d\geq 2. In the context of other equations, Shao–Wei–Zhang [55, 56] proved the existence of imploding solutions to the nonlinear wave and the relativistic Euler equations. We also point out to the numerical work of Biasi [1].

1.2 Main result

In [9] we managed to answer a question of [48] concerning the construction of non-radial imploding solutions for compressible Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. Our goal in this paper is to extend the previous construction to the case of the NLS equation (1.1). Broadly speaking, we are able to construct finite time imploding singularities with either:

  1. 1.

    smooth periodic initial data (Theorem 1.1).

  2. 2.

    smooth, non-radially symmetric initial data that does not vanish at infinity (Theorem 1.2).

The proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 starts with the transformation of the defocusing NLS equation into the compressible Euler equation via the Madelung transform (1.2). In order to perform the non-radial stability argument, we are inspired by our previous work [9]. We extend the new symmetry-breaking analysis that we developed there from 3D to higher dimensions and use it to perform the linearized non-radial stability estimate. This also requires a new angular repulsitivity condition on the profile to close the energy estimate. As a byproduct, we improve and generalize the techniques used in [46]. The key part of the non-linear stability argument hinges on involving the logarithm of the density, which leads to a new simplified version of the highest-order energy estimate without derivative losses. This energy estimate is new, and is a combination of the compressible Euler energy and the Hamiltonian of the defocusing NLS. The result in the periodic setting is obtained by introducing an argument involving a refined cut-off.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ψp,Sp\Psi_{p},S_{p} be self-similar profiles solving (1.10) for (d,p)=(8,3)(d,p)=(8,3) and satisfying (1.11)–(1.14), for some r>2r>2. Let T>0T>0 sufficiently small.

Then, there exists C∞C^{\infty} initial data v0v_{0} for which equation (1.1) on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} blows up at time TT in a self-similar manner. More concretely, for any fixed y∈𝕋dy\in\mathbb{T}^{d}, v⁡(y,t)=ρ​(y,t)​ei​Ψ​(y,t)v(y,t)=\sqrt{\rho}(y,t)e^{i\Psi(y,t)} with ρ∈ℝ+\rho\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, Ψ∈ℝ\Psi\in\mathbb{R}, we have:

limt→T−r​(T−t)1−2r​Ψ​((T−t)1r​y,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{2}{r}}\Psi\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right) =Ψp​(|y|),\displaystyle=\Psi_{p}(|y|),
limt→T−(α−1​r​(T−t)1−1r)1/α​ρ​((T−t)1r​y,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}\left(\alpha^{-1}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{1}{r}}\right)^{1/\alpha}\rho\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right) =Sp​(|y|)1/α.\displaystyle=S_{p}(|y|)^{1/\alpha}\,.

Moreover, there exists a finite codimension set of initial data satisfying the above conclusions.

Theorem 1.2.

Let Ψp,Sp\Psi_{p},S_{p} be self-similar profiles solving (1.10) for (d,p)=(8,3)(d,p)=(8,3) and satisfying (1.11)–(1.14), for some r>2r>2. Let T>0T>0 sufficiently small.

Then, there exists C∞C^{\infty} initial data v0v_{0} for which equation (1.1) on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} blows up at time TT in a self-similar manner. More concretely, for any fixed y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, v⁡(y,t)=ρ​(y,t)​ei​Ψ​(y,t)v(y,t)=\sqrt{\rho}(y,t)e^{i\Psi(y,t)} with ρ∈ℝ+\rho\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, Ψ∈ℝ\Psi\in\mathbb{R}, we have:

limt→T−r​(T−t)1−2r​Ψ​((T−t)1r​y,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{2}{r}}\Psi\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right) =Ψp​(|y|),\displaystyle=\Psi_{p}(|y|),
limt→T−(α−1​r​(T−t)1−1r)1/α​ρ​((T−t)1r​y,t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}\left(\alpha^{-1}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{1}{r}}\right)^{1/\alpha}\rho\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right) =Sp​(|y|)1/α.\displaystyle=S_{p}(|y|)^{1/\alpha}\,.

Moreover, there exists a finite codimension set of initial data satisfying the above conclusions.

Remark 1.3.

For simplicity, we have chosen to fix a particular instance of (d,p)(d,p). In principle, one could prove a similar result for other values of (d,p)(d,p) using a similar study of the angular repulsivity property, and even a larger class by means of a computer-assisted proof as in [7].

Remark 1.4.

Remark 1.5.

In recent years several works have been put forward in which it was proved that when one studies the long time dynamics of a periodic NLS the nature of the periodicity, namely the rationality or irrationality11 1 We say that a torus 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d} of periods T1,T2,…​TdT_{1},T_{2},\dots T_{d} is irrational if there is no non-zero vector w→=(w1,…,wd)∈ℤd\vec{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{d})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} such that ∑i=1dwi​Ti=0\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_{i}T_{i}=0. of the domain 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}, matters, see [33, 20, 22, 21, 57, 28, 30, 8, 35]. This physically makes sense since as time evolves the nonlinear solution starts seeing the different effects of the periodic boundary conditions. In our case, as one can gather from the conclusion of Theorem 1.1, we do not distinguish between a rational or irrational torus 𝕋d{\mathbb{T}}^{d}. This is because the blow up result we prove is localized and not close to the boundary. Of course we do not exclude that there could be other types of blow up mechanism that indeed are sensitive to the nature of the periodicity of the boundary, but the study of this phenomenon is not the scope of the present paper.

1.5 Organization of the paper

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is devoted to the study of the linearized operator around Sd,ΨdS_{d},\Psi_{d}, and it consists of the proof of Propositions 2.1, 2.3 and Lemma 2.2, concerning maximality, smoothness of the unstable modes and dissipativity of the linear operator. Section 3 upgrades the linear estimates to nonlinear, bootstrapping the bounds of the perturbation. Finally, the Appendix contains a proof of property (1.16) for the globally self-similar solution, as well as some other properties of the solution and some functional analytic results.

1.6 Notation

Throughout the paper we will use the following convention:

We will use CxC_{x} (resp. CC) to denote any constant that may depend on xx (resp. independent of all the other parameters). These constants may change from line to line but they are uniformly bounded by a universal constant dependent on xx (independent of all other parameters). Similarly, we will denote by X≲YX\lesssim Y and by X≲xYX\lesssim_{x}Y whenever X≤C​YX\leq CY and X≤Cx​YX\leq C_{x}Y for some CC, CxC_{x} respectively.

We use ∇lf\nabla^{l}f for the ll-th order tensor containing all ll order derivatives of ff. In the case where ff is a vector (typically f=Uf=U) then ∇lU\nabla^{l}U is a (l+1)(l+1)-th tensor. We also denote by |∇kf||\nabla^{k}f| its ℓ2\ell^{2} norm. Note that this norm controls all the derivatives accounting for reorderings of indices. For example, we have

|∇jf|2=∑β∈[3]j|∂βf|2≥(jj′)​|∂1j′∂2j−j′f|2.|\nabla^{j}f|^{2}=\sum_{\beta\in[3]^{j}}|\partial_{\beta}f|^{2}\geq\binom{j}{j^{\prime}}|\partial_{1}^{j^{\prime}}\partial_{2}^{j-j^{\prime}}f|^{2}.

Thus, we see that |∇jf||\nabla^{j}f| has a stronger control of the mixed derivatives by a combinatorial number, just because any mixed derivative appears multiple times in ∇jf\nabla^{j}f as the indices are reordered.

For β=(β1,β2​…,βK)\beta=(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}...,\beta_{K}), we let ∂β=∂β1,β2,β3​…​βK\partial_{\beta}=\partial_{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}...\beta_{K}}, and ∂β(j)=∂β1,β2,…​βj−1,βj+1​….βK\partial_{\beta^{(j)}}=\partial_{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},...\beta_{j-1},\beta_{j+1}....\beta_{K}} (that is, βj\beta_{j} denotes the jj-th component of β\beta and β(j)\beta^{(j)} denotes the subindex obtained by erasing the jj-th component in β\beta).

We will use yy as our self-similar variable and we will denote R=|y|R=|y| for the radius (given that rr is reserved, since 1/r1/r is the self-similar exponent of our ansatz). We will denote with R^\widehat{R} the unitary vector field in the radial direction, that is, R^=y|y|=yR\widehat{R}=\frac{y}{|y|}=\frac{y}{R}.

2 Linear estimates

2.1 Linear estimates for the truncated operator

This part is very similar as in [9, Section 2] except for the fact that we work with ∇Ψ\nabla\Psi instead of UU. We consider χ1​(x),χ2​(x)\chi_{1}(x),\chi_{2}(x) to be cut-offs with value 11 near the origin and transition regions [6/5,7/5][6/5,7/5] and [8/5,9/5][8/5,9/5] respectively. Notice that in the support of χ1\chi_{1} and χ2\chi_{2}, as long as s0s_{0} is sufficiently large, we have (Ψp,Sp)=(Ψd,Sd)(\Psi_{p},S_{p})=(\Psi_{d},S_{d}).

Using those cut-offs, we define the cut-off linear operator as:

ℒΨ,t=χ2​(yC0)​ℒΨ−J⁡(1−χ1​(yC0)),ℒS,t=χ2​(yC0)​ℒS−J⁡(1−χ1​(yC0)),\mathcal{L}_{\Psi,t}=\chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{L}_{\Psi}-J(1-\chi_{1}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})),\quad\mathcal{L}_{S,t}=\chi_{2}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})\mathcal{L}_{S}-J(1-\chi_{1}(\frac{y}{C_{0}})), (2.1)

where J,C0J,C_{0} are sufficiently large constant.

We will study the cut-off linearized operator ℒt=(ℒΨ,t,ℒS,t)\mathcal{L}_{t}=(\mathcal{L}_{\Psi,t},\mathcal{L}_{S,t}) in the space XX, which we define as follows. First, we consider X~\widetilde{X} to be the space HΨm+1​(Q,ℝ)×Hsm​(Q,ℝ)H^{m+1}_{\Psi}(Q,\mathbb{R})\times H^{m}_{s}(Q,\mathbb{R}) where the Ψ,s\Psi,s subscripts make reference to Ψ~\widetilde{\Psi} (vector field) and S~\widetilde{S} (scalar field). QQ is a cube centered at the origin of length 4​C04C_{0} and we take periodic boundary conditions. We select mm to be a sufficiently large integer. We define XX to be the subspace of X~\widetilde{X} formed by (Ψ,S)∈X~(\Psi,S)\in\widetilde{X} such that both UU and SS are compactly supported on B⁡(0,3​C0)B(0,3C_{0}). One can thus think of XX as a subspace of HΨm+1​(B⁡(0,3​C0),ℝ)×Hsm​(B⁡(0,3​C0),ℝ)H^{m+1}_{\Psi}(B(0,3C_{0}),\mathbb{R})\times H^{m}_{s}(B(0,3C_{0}),\mathbb{R}) with the appropriate vanishing conditions at the boundary. Whenever we take Fourier series of (Ψ,S)∈X(\Psi,S)\in X it should be understood that we do Fourier series on the cube QQ.

We put in our space XX the standard inner product

⟨(fΨ,fs),(gΨ,gs)⟩X=∫B⁡(0,3​C0)(∇m+1fΨ⋅∇m+1gΨ+∇mfs⋅∇mgs+fΨ⋅gΨ+fs​gs)\langle(f_{\Psi},f_{s}),(g_{\Psi},g_{s})\rangle_{X}=\int_{B(0,3C_{0})}\left(\nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi}\cdot\nabla^{m+1}g_{\Psi}+\nabla^{m}f_{s}\cdot\nabla^{m}g_{s}+f_{\Psi}\cdot g_{\Psi}+f_{s}g_{s}\right)

and we obtain the inherited norm

‖(fΨ,fs)‖X2=∫B⁡(0,3​C0)(|∇m+1fΨ|2+(∇mfs)2+|fΨ|2+fs2),\|(f_{\Psi},f_{s})\|_{X}^{2}=\int_{B(0,3C_{0})}\left(|\nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi}|^{2}+(\nabla^{m}f_{s})^{2}+|f_{\Psi}|^{2}+f_{s}^{2}\right), (2.2)

where ∇mfs\nabla^{m}f_{s} is an mm-tensor indexed by [d]m={1,2,…​d}m[d]^{m}=\{1,2,...d\}^{m} containing all possible combinations of directional derivatives. In the case of ∇m+1fΨ\nabla^{m+1}f_{\Psi}, we have an (m+1)(m+1)-tensor since we have an extra index indicating the component of the vector fΨf_{\Psi}.

Similar as in the [9], we have finite-dimension unstable space (Proposition 2.1) and smoothness of the eigenvectors in the unstable space (Proposition 2.3).

Proposition 2.1 ([9, Proposition 1.8]).

For δg\delta_{g} sufficiently small, mm sufficiently large and JJ defined in (2.1) sufficiently large, the following holds. Here (∇Ψ~,S~)(\nabla\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) corresponds to (U~,S~)(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{S}) in [9] with the properties of profile (1.16) and (1.15). The only difference is that, since we replace U~\widetilde{U} by ∇Ψ~\nabla\widetilde{\Psi}, the cut-off in the definition of ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t} (2.1) is performed on (Ψ~,S~)(\widetilde{\Psi},\widetilde{S}) instead of (U~,S~)(\widetilde{U},\widetilde{S}). Both the dissipativity and maximality work in a similar way since the change does not effect the leading order estimate (H˙Ψm+1​(Q)×H˙Sm​(Q)\dot{H}^{m+1}_{\Psi}(Q)\times\dot{H}^{m}_{S}(Q)). All the terms where derivatives enter the cut-off are bounded as error terms, so it is irrelevant if the cut-off is performed at the level of ∇Ψ~\nabla\widetilde{\Psi} or Ψ~\widetilde{\Psi}. The error terms are with lower derivative and can be controlled easily by taking KK sufficiently large.

3.3 Closing the low derivative energy bounds

First, let us make some observations regarding the parameters. We have that 1es0≪δlow≪1m≪1C0\frac{1}{e^{s_{0}}}\ll\delta_{\rm{low}}\ll\frac{1}{m}\ll\frac{1}{C_{0}}, where C0C_{0} is the cut-off length for the stability (constant in time in self-similar variables) and ese^{s} is the cut-off length for the damping of SdS_{d} (constant length LL in physical variables). The number mm corresponds to the number of derivatives needed for the linear stability. All those parameters are allowed to depend on ε,b,R0,m′\varepsilon,b,R_{0},m^{\prime}, which are the parameters of the low derivative energy bounds. Those low derivative energy bounds just depend on the profile and the parameter.

The objective of this and the next section will be to close the bootstrap assumptions at the middle and low derivative levels. The ingredients needed to close the low derivative are using the linear stability analysis for |y|≤C0|y|\leq C_{0} and trajectory estimates outside. The low derivative energy bounds follow from the energy estimates reminiscent of the compressible Euler structure (in contrast with the high derivative bounds, in which one needs to carefully combine the compressible Euler structure with the NLS one).

Up to this point, we have proved (3.14). This section is devoted to proving the low derivative energy estimate (3.6).

3.7 Topological argument section for the unstable modes

Now we are let to show Pu​n​s​(Ψt,St)≤δ32​e−ε⁡(s−s0).P_{uns}(\Psi_{t},S_{t})\leq\delta^{\frac{3}{2}}e^{-\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}. This comes from a standard topological argument. From the same topological argument in [9, Section 3.5], we have the following proposition.

Proposition 3.7.

There exists specific initial conditions {ai}\{a_{i}\} in (2.5), such that

‖Pu​n​s​(Ψt​(⋅,s),St​(⋅,s))‖X≤δ032​e−43​ε​(s−s0).\|P_{uns}(\Psi_{t}(\cdot,s),S_{t}(\cdot,s))\|_{X}\leq\delta_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}}e^{-\frac{4}{3}\varepsilon(s-s_{0})}.

Combining Propositions 3.1 and 3.7, we have Theorem 1.1.
